claims.text: SPS at 950 °C for 10 minutes under 30 MPa is the optimum process for the proposed Mg-10Al-5Cr-2Fe-2Ni alloy.
Powders smaller than 25 µm mechanically alloyed for 40 hours will induce solid-solution formation and reduce segregation.
At 950 °C, diffusion is sufficient for densification while Mg volatility remains acceptably low.
Below 800 °C, insufficient grain growth causes low density.
Mg volatility accelerates significantly above 1000 °C.
Rapid cooling after SPS will minimize grain growth and Mg evaporation.
High mixing entropy will stabilize a single-phase solid solution in the proposed alloy.
Entropy stabilization will suppress unstable phase transformations and elemental segregation.
High entropy lowers the solid-solution free energy and suppresses brittle intermetallic formation.
Al and Cr will preferentially oxidize at the surface during the sintering ramp to form Al2O3 and Cr2O3.
The resulting Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale will be dense and self-healing and will prevent bulk oxidation and corrosion.
The proposed process will produce a relative density above 98%.
The proposed process will produce a single-phase FCC or BCC microstructure.
The proposed alloy will have Vickers hardness above 250 HV.
The proposed alloy will reduce corrosion current density by at least 50% relative to standard sintered Mg alloys.
The stable surface oxide will be 50–100 nm thick.
Standard sintering at 850 °C gives less than 90% density and an unstable microstructure.
Sintering at 1050 °C causes severe Mg loss, porosity, and poor barrier properties.
Below 850 °C, relative density remains below 95% because diffusion is insufficient.
Above 1000 °C or below 10^-3 Pa, Mg loss exceeds 5%, causing pores and loss of mechanical integrity.

contradictions.description: The conditions are intended to prevent premature oxidation during heating, whereas the proposed mechanism requires Al and Cr to oxidize during the same sintering ramp to create the protective scale.

The stated composition is strongly Mg-dominant rather than a multi-principal-element alloy, yet the mechanism treats it as a high-entropy multi-principal system; it also incorrectly groups Al with the transition metals.
